title: Rental Payout Reconciliation Bridge
description: Compare an itemized expected payout with the bank receipt using your own records.
intro: Use this worksheet when a bank deposit differs from the booking receipts you expected. Enter one reporting currency and one clearly defined payout group. The calculator bridges gross receipts to an expected bank transfer; it does not retrieve transactions, interpret a platform dispute or determine tax treatment. All starting figures are illustrative and must be replaced with your records.

fields.label: Gross receipts in this payout group (currency units)
Refund deductions included in this payout (currency units)
Other deductions; negative means additions (currency units)
Actual bank receipt; negative means debit (currency units)

sections.title: Use one transaction group
sections.text: Start with a payout reference or a documented group of transfers. Record the report date and whether the gross figure includes taxes, cleaning or other guest charges. Do not combine bookings from one period with bank receipts from another without identifying the timing difference. The same currency must apply to every amount entered in this bridge.

sections.title: Understand the calculation
sections.text: Expected transfer equals gross receipts minus the four deduction categories. Other deductions can be negative when the documented item is an addition. The difference equals the actual bank receipt minus that expected amount. A positive difference means more money arrived than the model explains; a negative result means less arrived. Neither sign alone identifies the cause.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: The example starts with 1,000 currency units of receipts. Deductions are 100 in fees, 50 in refunds, 200 for a co-host and 25 in other adjustments. The expected transfer is 625. An actual receipt of 625 leaves no numerical difference. Replace every category before applying this structure to a real payout; the example does not represent a standard platform fee.

sections.title: Avoid double counting
sections.text: A refund already removed from the gross input must not be deducted again. Likewise, a manager fee paid separately from another bank account does not belong in this transfer bridge unless it actually reduced this payout. Keep each source entry beside the field it supports. If one deduction relates to an earlier booking, preserve that booking reference rather than forcing it into the current stay.

sections.title: Resolve the difference
sections.text: Compare the result with payment-provider statements and bank records. Investigate processing dates, currency conversion, withheld balances and routing before describing money as missing. Do not change a payout method simply to make the worksheet balance. Record the identified explanation or an open support case, then send the reconciled evidence to the person responsible for the books.

note: An arithmetic match does not prove every transaction is valid or correctly classified. Use actual payout and bank records.

title: Reservation Change Cash-Difference Calculator
description: Separate a booking-price change from the remaining amount to collect or return.
intro: A reservation amendment changes the price agreement, but the cash still due also depends on prior payments and approved credits. Use this calculator to keep those two questions separate. Enter original and revised components in the same currency, then record payments already received and credits that are genuinely approved. It does not apply a platform cancellation policy or initiate a charge.

netDue: Net due; negative means potential refund

sections.title: Document the accepted amendment
sections.text: Use the actual reservation and proposed or accepted change record. Distinguish an estimate sent in a message from a change confirmed through the applicable booking process. Identify which fees or taxes change and which remain fixed. The calculator accepts your figures; it does not establish that a guest owes an amount merely because you enter it.

sections.title: Read the two differences
sections.text: Original total and revised total each sum lodging, fees and taxes. The booking-price change is revised total minus original total. Net due is revised total less additional approved credit and payments already received. A negative net due indicates that the entered payments and credit exceed the revised charge, rather than instructing you to issue a refund automatically.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: The original example totals 750 currency units and the revised components total 960. The booking price increases by 210. Because 750 has already been received and an additional 20 credit is approved, the remaining modeled balance is 190. The distinction matters: charging another 210 would ignore the separate approved credit in this example.

sections.title: Use payment records consistently
sections.text: Enter payments on the same basis as the revised price. If a prior refund has already reduced payments retained, use the net amount still held and document that treatment. Do not both net the refund from payments and enter it again as a credit. Do not mix the guest’s total with the owner’s net payout after platform fees.

sections.title: Confirm the actual transaction
sections.text: Review the platform or payment provider’s final calculation before charging or refunding. Timing, policy, taxes and fees may produce a different actual result. Keep the accepted amendment, transaction confirmation and worksheet together. An unresolved discrepancy should remain an open item for the responsible operator or adviser rather than being disguised with an unexplained balancing entry.

note: Positive net due is a modeled balance, not payment authorization. Verify the accepted change and provider rules before acting.

title: Owner Cash-Allocation Worksheet
description: Model a discretionary allocation after your designated exclusions, bills and reserve.
intro: This calculator subtracts amounts you designate from a cash balance and shows the remaining modeled allocation. It does not decide whether guest funds, deposits or other money may legally be distributed. Obtain the relevant agreement and professional guidance first, and enter excluded amounts yourself. The example is a bookkeeping planning exercise, not a recommendation to withdraw funds.

fields.label: Pending bills to retain cash for (currency units)

sections.title: Define the starting balance
sections.text: Use a dated account or ledger balance and identify its scope. Available bank cash and a statement’s ending balance can differ because transactions are pending. Avoid combining money from separate owners or accounts without a reconciled basis. Record the source and date so another reviewer knows exactly which funds were included.

sections.title: Designate exclusions independently
sections.text: The excluded-funds input is supplied by you after reviewing applicable obligations. The calculator cannot identify trust money, refundable deposits, taxes, future-stay receipts or contractual restrictions. It does not turn an amount into distributable cash by leaving the field at zero. Keep the basis for each exclusion outside the calculator in the responsible records.

sections.title: Understand the result
sections.text: The model subtracts excluded funds, pending bills and the selected reserve from recorded cash. A positive remainder is displayed as the modeled ceiling. A negative remainder displays a zero ceiling and a shortfall. This separates a cash gap from a negative proposed distribution and helps the reviewer see which retained amounts exceed the starting balance.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: With 3,000 currency units in cash, 500 designated as excluded, 1,000 retained for bills and a 2,000 reserve, the modeled balance is negative 500. The allocation ceiling is zero and the shortfall is 500. If the reserve were reduced, the arithmetic would change, but that would not establish that reducing it is prudent or permitted.

sections.title: Review before a transfer
sections.text: Reconcile outstanding payments and verify who may approve an actual distribution. Check whether another owner, lender or agreement imposes restrictions not represented here. Save the assumptions and approval date with any resulting transaction. A numerical ceiling is only as complete as the obligations entered; it is not evidence that an omitted bill or liability disappeared.

note: User-designated exclusions and reserve are assumptions. This tool does not determine legal availability or authorize distributions.

title: Same-Day Turnover Window Calculator
description: Compare cleaning, inspection and between-job travel minutes with a specific arrival window.
intro: This is a same-day capacity screen for similar turnovers within one shared time window. It shows both total team-minutes and the estimated longest team assignment when jobs are divided as evenly as possible. It does not build a route or guarantee readiness. All tasks are assumed sequential within a team, and actual addresses, access delays and differing job sizes still need a schedule.

fields.label: Travel between jobs on one team (minutes)
Time from earliest start to required finish (minutes)

singleJob: Cleaning plus inspection for one job

sections.title: Use the same-day window
sections.text: Measure from the earliest realistic access time to the required completion time for this group of jobs. Do not use a week’s total working hours. Enter teams that are actually available during this window, not every person on the roster. A team is treated as one work unit with the stated per-job duration.

sections.title: Read aggregate and team results together
sections.text: Each job uses cleaning plus inspection minutes. The model adds travel between jobs after the first job assigned to each team. Combined capacity is teams multiplied by the window. The longest balanced assignment uses the ceiling of jobs divided by teams. Negative team headroom warns that the equal-duration jobs do not fit that assignment even if aggregate capacity appears sufficient.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Three jobs each need 80 minutes of cleaning and 10 of inspection. Two teams have 180 minutes, and between-job travel takes 20. Modeled labor is 290 team-minutes versus 360 of aggregate capacity. However, one team receives two jobs: 90 plus 20 plus 90 equals 200 minutes. That team is 20 minutes beyond the window despite aggregate spare capacity.

sections.title: Replace the uniform-job assumption
sections.text: A larger property, late checkout or separate inspection crew can invalidate equal-duration assumptions. Record actual addresses and earliest access times in a scheduling tool. Add realistic delivery, key and supply tasks to the inputs or schedule rather than hiding them inside apparent slack. This screen cannot establish that an individual contractor can perform work simultaneously at different properties.

sections.title: Use the result for a dispatch decision
sections.text: If either aggregate slack or team headroom is negative, revise the plan before promising readiness. Consider authorized staffing, timing or scope changes and recalculate with their actual effects. Even a positive result needs route and task confirmation. Save the version used for dispatch and compare actual durations afterward to improve future estimates without representing the result as a guarantee.

note: Capacity screen only. Uniform job times and balanced assignment do not prove route feasibility or guaranteed readiness.

title: Rental Linen Par and Inventory-Gap Calculator
description: Estimate compatible sheet and bath sets across use, laundry and chosen spare rounds.
intro: Use complete, compatible sets as the unit for this inventory calculation. The model starts with one sheet set per bed and one bath set per planned guest, then adds your chosen laundry and spare rounds. It does not select a hygiene standard or predict laundry turnaround. Enter the actual operational rounds needed for your property and keep incompatible sizes separate.

fields.label: Beds using one complete sheet set each (whole beds)
Guests using one complete bath set each (whole guests)
Additional full rounds in laundry (whole rounds)
Additional spare rounds you choose (whole rounds)
Compatible sheet sets on hand (whole sets)
Complete bath sets on hand (whole sets)

rounds: Total use, laundry and spare rounds

sections.title: Define a complete set
sections.text: Decide what belongs in a sheet or bath set before counting inventory. The calculator treats each set as interchangeable within the group. A king set cannot automatically replace a twin set, and loose towels are not necessarily complete bath sets. Run separate calculations for incompatible bed sizes or different service standards rather than pooling everything into one number.

sections.title: Model laundry overlap
sections.text: A laundry round is an additional full turnover quantity unavailable because it is being processed. The spare-round input represents a separate reserve you choose for damage, delays or other needs. Neither input is a recommendation. Check actual laundry pickup, wash, drying and return timing before deciding how many rounds can be unavailable together.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Three beds and four guests require three sheet sets and four bath sets for one use round. One additional laundry round and one chosen spare round bring the total to three rounds: nine sheet sets and twelve bath sets. With eight compatible sheet sets and ten complete bath sets on hand, the model shows gaps of one and two sets respectively.

sections.title: Count usable stock honestly
sections.text: Exclude stained, damaged, incompatible or unavailable items from on-hand quantities unless they can actually be used in the modeled cycle. Avoid counting the same set at two properties or both at the laundry and on the shelf. Keep the inventory date and the definition of each set with the result so another team member can repeat the count.

sections.title: Convert the gap into an order
sections.text: Check package contents, sizes and actual delivery timing before purchasing. A displayed gap is measured in complete sets, not retail packages. Review storage and replacement needs separately. After the next busy turnover period, compare the model with actual shortages or excess stock and adjust the chosen rounds; the calculation does not guarantee that every laundry disruption is covered.

note: Inventory arithmetic only. Run separate groups for incompatible linen sizes and define complete sets consistently.

title: Rental Consumable Reorder Planner
description: Estimate a reorder point and whole-pack order from your usage and lead-time assumptions.
intro: This planner uses one consumable measured in one consistent unit, such as rolls, pods or bottles. Enter observed use per occupied night, expected occupied nights per week and delivery lead time. The result is a stock-planning calculation, not a demand forecast or supplier guarantee. Review shortages and actual consumption before treating the assumptions as a recurring purchasing rule.

fields.label: Units in one purchasable pack (whole units)

sections.title: Choose a consistent usage basis
sections.text: Occupied nights here are the combined nights for the inventory group, not necessarily calendar nights at one property. Keep the units-per-night measure consistent with that group. If you track use per guest-night, convert both inputs to that basis before using the planner. Do not mix guest-nights and property-nights in the same calculation.

sections.title: Understand both stock figures
sections.text: The reorder point equals modeled use during delivery lead time plus your chosen safety stock. Inventory position is usable on-hand stock plus confirmed units on order. The suggested order compares that position with target-week use plus safety stock and rounds upward to whole packs. It does not account for an unconfirmed order or a shipment arriving after the need date. Packs to target is a quantity comparison, not an automatic instruction to order before reaching your reorder point.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Two units per occupied night across ten occupied nights per week give twenty units of weekly use. With a two-week lead time and ten safety units, the reorder point is fifty units. Twenty-five on hand plus fifteen on order make forty. A four-week target plus safety stock is ninety, leaving fifty units to purchase, rounded to five packs of twelve.

sections.title: Interpret zero use and lead time
sections.text: When modeled use is zero, on-hand coverage in weeks is not defined; the calculator displays that instead of dividing by zero. Safety stock can still affect a target. Zero delivery lead time is allowed as an assumption, but it is not a supplier promise. Test a delayed delivery or busier occupancy case before relying on a small inventory buffer.

sections.title: Review the actual purchase
sections.text: Check pack size, usable storage, expiration and delivery date. Confirm that on-order stock has not been counted twice after receiving it. Keep a dated usage sample and investigate unusual consumption rather than automatically raising the order every time. A numerical reorder point supports purchasing decisions without determining which product or supplier is appropriate.

note: Whole-pack rounding may create stock above the target. Lead time and expected use are entered assumptions, not guarantees.

title: Maintenance Quote Cost Comparison
description: Normalize two itemized cost estimates without ranking contractor quality or scope.
intro: Compare the arithmetic in two maintenance proposals after confirming that their work scopes are comparable. Each estimate has a callout charge, labor rate and hours, materials, material markup and a separately entered tax amount. No tax rule or provider quality is inferred. The lower modeled total is not automatically the better proposal, and estimated hours are not a fixed-price commitment.

fields.label: Quote A quoted tax amount (currency units)
Quote B quoted tax amount (currency units)

difference: A minus B; positive means A costs more

sections.title: Compare scope before numbers
sections.text: List the defect, diagnosis, proposed work, parts, disposal and completion evidence in each proposal. A repair and a replacement may address the same symptom differently. Identify exclusions and required approvals. Do not describe the proposals as equivalent merely because they concern the same appliance or room; this calculator does not evaluate technical adequacy.

sections.title: Use the stated fee structure
sections.text: The model adds callout, labor rate multiplied by hours, materials including the entered markup and the quoted tax amount. If a provider already includes markup in its materials figure, enter zero markup to avoid counting it twice. If a visit charge includes labor time, adjust the hours to the separately chargeable amount and document the interpretation.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Quote A uses a fifty-unit callout, two hours at sixty, one hundred of materials with twenty percent markup and no separately entered tax. Its total is 290. Quote B uses thirty, two hours at seventy and ninety of materials with ten percent markup, totaling 269. The difference is twenty-one currency units, before considering scope or contractual differences.

sections.title: Stress-test estimated hours
sections.text: A time-and-materials estimate can change when work takes longer. Recalculate with a plausible higher number of hours taken from the provider’s explanation, rather than inventing a universal contingency. Check whether the contract has a cap, minimum charge or further authorization requirement that this simple model does not represent. Obtain a revised quote when the scope changes.

sections.title: Keep selection separate
sections.text: Review qualifications, insurance where relevant, scheduling, warranties and the actual work specification outside the calculator. Record the reason for choosing a provider, including any nonprice factors. Do not present the output as a contractor ranking or proof that a repair is necessary. Save the accepted scope and final invoice so estimated and actual costs can be compared later.

note: Cost comparison only. Enter tax from the proposal; no jurisdictional tax treatment, repair necessity or provider quality is determined.

title: Payout Currency Reconciliation Calculator
description: Compare a converted payout with a bank entry using an entered rate and destination-currency fees.
intro: Use this calculator to reproduce a currency conversion already documented by a payment provider or to check an explicitly labeled assumption. It does not supply an exchange rate or recommend when to exchange money. Enter the rate as destination-currency units for one source-currency unit. All fees and the bank receipt must be expressed in the destination currency.

fields.label: Payout amount in source currency; refunds may be negative
Destination units per one source unit
Actual bank amount in destination currency; debit may be negative

sections.title: Name both currencies in your records
sections.text: Record the source and destination currency codes beside the saved calculation. A number alone does not identify whether the rate should be multiplied or divided. This calculator always multiplies the source amount by destination units per source unit. Convert an inverse quote before entering it, using the provider’s documented rate rather than a guessed current rate.

sections.title: Trace the actual conversion
sections.text: Identify which institution performed the conversion and which fees appear separately. A platform, intermediary and receiving bank can each have a different role. Enter only fees expressed in the destination currency. If a fee was deducted from the source amount first, either use the net source amount with an explanation or reconcile that fee separately; do not deduct it twice.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: A source payout of 1,000 multiplied by a rate of 1.10 produces 1,100 destination units. Subtracting five destination units of fees gives an expected bank amount of 1,095. A bank receipt of 1,095 leaves zero difference. These are illustrative numbers, not an available exchange quote or a forecast of future conversion costs.

sections.title: Handle refunds and rounding
sections.text: A negative source amount can represent a refund or reversal and produces a negative converted amount at a positive rate. The rate itself must be greater than zero. Results display two decimal places while calculations retain precision internally. Some currencies and providers use different minor-unit conventions; reconcile the provider’s actual rounding rather than assuming every currency uses two decimal places.

sections.title: Investigate an unexplained difference
sections.text: Check value dates, fee currency, rate direction and whether several transfers were combined in one bank entry. Keep the original provider and bank records with any explanation. A remaining difference is not by itself proof of an error or unauthorized charge. Refer accounting or tax conversion-method questions to the responsible adviser; this tool only applies the entered arithmetic.

note: Reconciliation only. The rate is user-entered; displayed rounding may differ from a provider or currency’s minor-unit rules.

title: Turnover Contract Break-Even Calculator
description: Compare a monthly retainer plus a per-turn charge with a purely per-turn quote.
intro: Two cleaning proposals can have different cost structures even when they cover the same work. This calculator compares one monthly retainer plus a per-turn charge against another per-turn charge. Enter the same property, service scope and month for both proposals. The starting values illustrate the arithmetic; they are not market prices.

fields.label: Monthly retainer for option A (currency units)
Additional charge per turnover for A
Charge per turnover for option B
Expected turnovers in the month (whole turnovers)

crossing: Equal-cost turnover count, when rates differ

sections.title: Match the scope first
sections.text: Before entering a rate, compare what the quote covers: linen handling, supply replenishment, inspection, travel and unusual checkout conditions. A lower number for a smaller scope is not a saving on equivalent work. Add known compulsory charges consistently or record them outside the model. The calculator treats the two entered service structures as complete for the selected month.

sections.title: Read the crossover
sections.text: Option A equals the monthly retainer plus its per-turn charge multiplied by turnover count. Option B is its per-turn charge multiplied by the same count. Equal cost occurs at retainer divided by the difference between B’s and A’s per-turn rates. If the rates are equal, there is no unique crossover. A negative crossover does not describe an attainable nonnegative workload.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: With a 300 retainer, 60 per turn for A and 100 per turn for B, ten turns cost 900 under A and 1,000 under B. The numerical crossover is 7.5 turns. Because actual turnovers are whole jobs, compare seven and eight jobs individually before describing a threshold. At eight turns A is 780 and B is 800.

sections.title: Test a quieter month
sections.text: Replace the expected count with a plausible quieter month and retain the same quoted rates. At five turns the example changes to 600 for A and 500 for B. This does not determine which contract to sign: minimum terms, cancellation provisions and the provider’s ability to deliver the work remain separate facts. Save the dated proposals alongside the scenarios.

note: Costs exclude anything not entered. A fractional crossover is a mathematical point, not a billable job.

title: Rental Replacement Reserve Worksheet
description: Spread a chosen replacement target over the months remaining in your plan.
intro: Build a simple reserve schedule for one group of comparable items, such as mattresses or patio chairs. Enter your chosen future replacement cost, item count, months until purchase and cash already assigned to that group. This model spreads the remaining gap evenly. It does not predict product life or establish an accounting depreciation schedule.

fields.label: Planned future cost per item (currency units)
Cash already assigned to this group

monthly: Equal monthly contribution to close gap

sections.title: Define one replacement group
sections.text: Use items with a shared replacement date and cost basis. Separate groups with different sizes, delivery requirements or purchase timing. Enter a future cost that you selected from an actual quote or documented assumption, including the charges you intend to fund. A current retail listing is not a promise that the same price will be available when the purchase occurs.

sections.title: Count only assigned cash
sections.text: Use money specifically assigned to this group in your own plan. The worksheet does not determine whether the cash is available to spend or subject to other obligations. If several reserve worksheets are used, do not count the same cash in each. Maintain a separate register connecting the amount entered here to the overall cash plan.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Four items at 450 each create a target of 1,800. With 600 already assigned, the remaining gap is 1,200. Over 24 months, the equal monthly contribution is 50. If assigned cash exceeds the target, the contribution becomes zero and the surplus is shown separately. The model does not withdraw money or move it between accounts.

sections.title: Revisit the plan when facts change
sections.text: Update the worksheet if a quote changes, an item fails earlier or the purchase date moves. A shorter remaining period can substantially increase the monthly amount. Keep the prior version so the reason for the change is visible. Interest, inflation and tax treatment are not modeled; incorporate those questions separately when they matter to the decision.

note: The purchase date and future cost are user assumptions. Keep each reserve group separate to avoid counting cash twice.

title: Booking Channel Net-Proceeds Comparison
description: Compare two entered fee structures against one equal gross booking amount.
intro: Use this comparison when two booking routes quote different percentage and fixed charges. Enter the same gross booking amount for both and identify which costs actually apply to each route. The result is a narrow net-proceeds comparison, not a claim that a direct booking or particular platform is always better.

fields.label: Same gross booking amount for both routes

sections.title: Choose a consistent gross basis
sections.text: Confirm the base on which each percentage actually applies. This model applies both rates to the single gross figure entered. If a provider applies its fee to a different subtotal, calculate that amount from its actual statement before using an equivalent rate here, or compare the statement manually. Do not mix a guest’s full bill with an owner’s already reduced payout.

sections.title: Include only relevant fixed costs
sections.text: The fixed-charge fields represent amounts allocated to this one booking. They may include a transaction charge or a documented allocation you choose. Do not allocate a monthly subscription in one route while ignoring an equivalent cost in the other without identifying the difference. Advertising, refunds and customer-service work are outside the model unless you deliberately include their amounts.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: On a gross amount of 1,000, route A at three percent with no fixed charge costs 30 and leaves 970. Route B at 2.9 percent plus 20 costs 49 and leaves 951. The modeled proceeds difference is 19 in favor of A. These sample percentages are illustrative inputs, not current fees for any named provider.

sections.title: Keep commercial differences visible
sections.text: Payment timing, distribution reach, dispute handling and booking terms can differ even when the arithmetic favors one route. Keep those facts beside the cost comparison. A negative net result is possible if entered charges exceed gross receipts; it signals the input scenario rather than a payment instruction. Reconcile the actual completed booking against its provider statement.

note: Percentage charges use the entered gross amount. The example names no provider and contains no current fee claim.

title: Stay-Length Turnover Cost Calculator
description: See how one fixed turnover cost is spread across different stay lengths.
intro: A fixed cleaning or preparation cost creates a different cost per occupied night for a two-night stay and a seven-night stay. This tool spreads one entered turnover cost over two stay lengths and adds your selected variable cost per occupied night. It does not set a nightly price or apply a booking platform’s fee rules.

fields.label: Variable operating cost per occupied night

totalA: Modeled operating cost for stay A
perNightA: Cost per occupied night for A
totalB: Modeled operating cost for stay B
perNightB: Cost per occupied night for B
difference: A minus B cost per occupied night

sections.title: Define the cost categories
sections.text: Put costs incurred once per completed stay in the turnover field. Put the selected costs that change with each occupied night in the variable field. A supply item used once per booking should not also be included per night. The model assumes the entered turnover cost is the same for both lengths; if a longer stay changes the cleaning scope, calculate that difference separately.

sections.title: Read total and nightly cost together
sections.text: Total cost equals turnover cost plus nightly variable cost multiplied by stay length. Cost per occupied night divides that total by the number of nights. A longer stay usually spreads the fixed component more widely, but its total cost can still be higher. Neither result measures revenue, margin or the cost of nights left empty around the reservation.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: With a fixed turnover cost of 140 and variable cost of 20 per night, two nights cost 180 in total or 90 per occupied night. Seven nights cost 280 in total or 40 per occupied night. The difference is 50 per occupied night. This is the effect of the selected cost assumptions, not a recommendation for a minimum-stay rule.

sections.title: Apply the scenario carefully
sections.text: Compare the result with the actual reservation pattern, staffing arrangement and service scope. If a linen change or mid-stay service occurs only after a certain length, the simple model needs a separate calculation. Keep taxes, debt service and other omitted costs visible elsewhere. Review the platform’s current settings before making any operational change; this tool does not change a listing.

note: Only the entered cost categories are modeled. Cost per occupied night is not a recommended selling price.

title: Rental Project Budget and Contingency Worksheet
description: Compare committed work with a selected contingency and the available project budget.
intro: Use this worksheet for a defined furnishing or maintenance project with a base quote and known additional costs. Apply a contingency percentage that you choose to the combined cost base, then compare the result with the budget. This is an arithmetic scenario; the percentage does not establish how much uncertainty a project actually carries.

fields.label: Delivery and installation excluded from base

sections.title: Establish the base quote
sections.text: Identify the dated quote, included work and exclusions before entering the base amount. The delivery field is for charges not already included in that quote. The other-cost field is for known items rather than a balancing amount. If a vendor revises the scope, update the underlying quote reference so the worksheet can still be traced to the actual proposal.

sections.title: Choose what the allowance covers
sections.text: This tool applies the chosen percentage to base work, delivery and other known costs combined. It does not apply the percentage only to labor or to selected line items. Record the intended purpose of the allowance and keep known work out of it. An uncertainty that can be priced now belongs in the cost subtotal rather than being hidden in an arbitrary percentage.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Base work of 5,000, delivery and installation of 600, and other known costs of 400 produce a 6,000 subtotal. A ten-percent selected allowance adds 600, creating a planned total of 6,600. Against a 6,500 budget, the variance is negative 100. A negative figure means the modeled total exceeds the entered budget.

sections.title: Track commitments separately
sections.text: A budget is not a bank balance or proof that spending is approved. Keep signed commitments, deposits and completed payments in a separate project record. When an allowance is used for identified work, revise the known-cost subtotal and decide whether any remaining allowance should change. Avoid adding the same expense to both committed costs and the contingency balance.

note: The contingency is user-selected and applies to the entire known-cost subtotal. No risk allowance is recommended.

title: Rental Utility Usage Period Normalizer
description: Compare meter usage per calendar day across two unequal billing periods.
intro: Utility bills covering different numbers of days are difficult to compare using totals alone. This tool divides each period’s recorded consumption by its calendar days and shows the daily difference. Use the same meter, measurement unit and reading basis. The result normalizes period length; it does not isolate the effect of guests, weather or equipment.

fields.label: Recorded consumption in period A (same units)
Calendar days in period A (whole days)
Recorded consumption in period B (same units)
Calendar days in period B (whole days)

percent: Change from A, when A is nonzero

sections.title: Match the readings
sections.text: Use consumption, such as electricity units or water volume, rather than the bill’s currency total. Charges can contain fixed fees and adjustments unrelated to consumption. Confirm whether the readings are actual or estimated and keep that basis with the worksheet. Do not compare different meters or different measurement units merely because both bills use the same provider.

sections.title: Count the billing days
sections.text: Use the period length supported by the bill or the dated meter readings. A calendar month label does not establish that every bill covers the same number of days. The calculator requires a positive whole-day count and does not decide whether a provider includes one or both endpoint dates. Follow the source record’s stated period consistently.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Period A uses 900 units over 30 days, giving 30 units per day. Period B uses 840 units over 28 days, also giving 30 units per day. The lower total in B does not represent a reduction in daily consumption. The normalized difference is zero and the percentage change is zero. This demonstrates why totals alone can mislead.

sections.title: Investigate rather than infer causation
sections.text: A daily difference may reflect weather, occupancy, leaks, equipment changes or a corrected reading. The worksheet does not identify which factor caused it. Use separate records and qualified follow-up for the actual question. If A has zero consumption, a percentage change from A is undefined; the absolute daily difference remains available. Keep tariffs and bill costs in a separate comparison.

note: Use one measurement unit throughout. Period normalization does not establish efficiency or explain a usage change.

title: Rental Maintenance Backlog Capacity Calculator
description: Compare planned task hours with the weekly hours assigned to a maintenance backlog.
intro: Use this capacity screen for a backlog that has already been assessed and assigned estimated work hours. It subtracts recurring work from a team’s scheduled weekly hours and compares the remaining capacity with the one-time backlog. It does not prioritize safety issues, authorize repairs or build a contractor schedule.

fields.label: Scheduled hours per person per week
Team hours reserved for recurring work per week

gross: Total scheduled team hours per week

sections.title: Build the backlog estimate
sections.text: Use task-level estimates from the people qualified to assess the work. Include access, preparation, cleanup and expected coordination where relevant. Separate work that needs a specialist from tasks the entered team can perform. The tool treats all backlog hours as compatible with the remaining team capacity, so a mixed trade backlog needs separate calculations or a real schedule.

sections.title: Reserve recurring work once
sections.text: Enter recurring work as a total for the team, not per person. Scheduled team hours equal worker count multiplied by hours per person. Remaining capacity is that total less recurring hours. If the remainder is zero or negative, the model cannot calculate a completion time; increasing the calendar horizon does not create capacity that has not been assigned.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Two workers scheduled for 20 hours each provide 40 team hours weekly. Reserving 24 hours for recurring work leaves 16 for the backlog. A 48-hour backlog takes three continuous-capacity weeks. If only 15 hours remain, the continuous result is 3.2 weeks and four whole weekly periods are required. Partial-week arithmetic does not specify a completion day.

sections.title: Check dependencies before promising a date
sections.text: Parts delivery, guest access, trade availability and task sequence can make elapsed time longer than this capacity screen. Record those constraints separately and review urgent work through the appropriate process. After each work period, update the remaining backlog with completed tasks and revised estimates. Do not count a task as finished solely because its estimated hours have been spent.

note: Uniform available hours are assumed. No completion date is guaranteed; tasks may require different workers or dependencies.

title: Rental Payment Installment Balance Worksheet
description: Reconcile an agreed total against payments and an approved adjustment before dividing a remaining balance.
intro: Use this worksheet to review a payment schedule that the parties have already agreed. Enter the total, net payments retained, any approved reduction and the number of remaining equal installments. The tool calculates a balance and a rounding-aware split; it does not establish a debt, change a reservation or authorize collection.

regular: First installments, rounded down to cents

sections.title: Use the accepted schedule
sections.text: Match the total to the accepted reservation or written agreement and identify what it includes. Enter net payments retained after any prior refunds, and do not deduct those refunds again as a new reduction. A proposed discount is not an approved adjustment. Keep the agreement, provider payment record and any accepted change together so the arithmetic can be reviewed.

sections.title: Understand the split
sections.text: The remaining balance is the greater of zero and total less retained payments and the approved reduction. The tool divides the balance into the entered count, rounding the first installments down to cents and assigning the remainder to the final one. It assumes a currency with two decimal places. It does not calculate interest, late fees or a provider’s installment rules.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: An agreed total of 1,200 less 300 retained and a 25 approved reduction leaves 875. Across three installments, the first two are 291.66 each and the last is 291.68. Together they equal 875. If retained payments plus the reduction exceed the total, the balance is zero and the excess appears separately instead of creating negative installments.

sections.title: Reconcile the actual collection
sections.text: Confirm due dates and allowed payment methods through the relevant booking or payment system. A balance on this screen does not make a charge permissible. After each actual payment, update the retained amount and remaining count from the provider record. If a dispute or pending payment exists, identify it separately rather than treating an uncertain amount as settled cash.

note: Two-decimal currency rounding only. This worksheet neither authorizes a charge nor applies platform-specific payment rules.
